newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N., EU aid chiefs ask access to Zaire refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.N., EU aid chiefs ask access to Zaire refugees.

text.p: Heads of United Nations aid agencies and the European Union's humanitarian chief on Friday appealed to Zairean government and rebel forces to allow relief workers access to refugees and displaced people in the country.
The appeal, the text of which was released in Geneva, was directed at representatives of the two sides who are due to meet in South Africa on Saturday for peace talks.
The aid chiefs urged participants "to fully consider the urgent humanitarian needs of hundreds of thousands of refugees and displaced Zaireans stranded in the war zone".

They added: "We call on the parties to respect humanitarian principles and the Geneva Conventions, to allow aid agencies free access to refugees and displaced persons, among whom are thousands of children, and to enable aid workers to reach and assist them."

The appeal was signed by EU commissioner for humanitarian affairs Emma Bonino, Sadako Ogata of the UNHCR refugee agency, Carole Bellamy of the U.N. children's fund UNICEF, and by an official of the Rome-based World Food Programme on behalf of its Executive Director Catherine Bertini.

Aid officials have expressed special concern that the insurgents led by Laurent Kabila who now control about one quarter of the country have declined to authorise a quick evacuation of refugees from near Kisangani.

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire has refused to allow refugees, mainly Rwandan Hutus, to be moved into the city, arguing that they include militiamen responsible for the massacre of Tutsis in Rwanda.

U.N. aid agencies say the refugees, who have been fleeing for fear of reprisals from Kabila's Tutsi-dominated fighters, are too weak to walk back to a collection point where the Alliance says they should gather.

"Aid agencies should be able to work without any restrictions to save many thousands of refugees and displaced persons who are exhausted after months of roaming desperately through the jungle and whose lives are currently hanging by a thread," the U.N.-EU appeal said.
All four signatories visited camps in eastern Zaire where the refugees collected earlier this year before the insurgents' advance on Kisangani last month.
"We have witnessed the plight of the refugees ourselves," they said. "We are now trying to help them and prepare for repatriation."

The UNHCR said on Friday that at least 120 refugees were dying every day in two makeshift camps south of Kisangani, where some 80,000 people were gathered and to which it and other aid bodies had been allowed access by the rebels since Tuesday.

"At least 20,000 children, women, sick and elderly are in urgent need of evacuation," UNHCR spokeswoman Pam O'Toole told a news briefing. She said negotiations were under way with the rebels for these to be moved through Kisangani airport.

The agency aims to bring them back to the Rwandan border from where they can be moved back to their home country -- following several hundred thousand Hutus who went back after the rebels overran camps in the frontier area last year.

O'Toole said planes bringing aid to Kisangani from the border town of Goma "are returning empty and we need to make use of them". If the rebels gave the go-ahead, each flight could bring out 150 refugees, she added.
